title: Forgery in property documents - how criminal and civil cases run parallel
p1:
Someone forges your property documents and tries to claim ownership. What happens next?

Many people assume that filing a criminal complaint will automatically settle the ownership dispute. That's a costly misconception.
p2:
Here's something many property owners don't realise: criminal and civil proceedings can run simultaneously over the same forged document.

The criminal case focuses on whether someone deliberately forged documents, used them dishonestly, or committed fraud. The civil case focuses on who actually has legal rights over the property and whether a disputed transaction should be declared invalid.
p3:
Think of it this way: one case addresses the alleged crime; the other protects your property rights.

A criminal conviction does not automatically transfer ownership to the genuine owner. Similarly, winning a civil ownership dispute does not necessarily establish someone's criminal guilt.

That's why simply filing an FIR may not be enough. Depending on the circumstances, you may also need to seek civil remedies, such as a declaration that a forged deed is invalid, cancellation of the document, or an injunction preventing further transfers.

The practical lesson? Preserve original documents, registration records, signatures, and transaction evidence. Consider both legal routes rather than assuming one will resolve everything.
conclusion: If someone forges a property deed, do you think pursuing criminal proceedings alone is enough, or should the genuine owner also initiate a separate civil case? Share your perspective.
